desc:
prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. You may make as many transactions as you like; a transaction is one purchase of a single share followed by a sale on a strictly later day. You can hold at most one share at a time.

After you sell on day s, you must rest for c full days: the earliest day on which you may buy again is s + c + 1. Return the maximum total profit.

Example: prices = [1,2,3,0,2]. With c = 1 the answer is 3 (buy 1, sell 2, rest, buy 0, sell 2). With c = 2 it is 2 (for example buy 1 and sell 3, or buy 0 and sell 2).
hints: Think of each day as ending in one of two situations: holding a share, or holding nothing. What extra information does the cooldown add?

Let free[i] be the best profit after day i with no share in hand (a sale on day i counts). You may only buy on day i using the profit free[i - c - 1], because the last sale has to be at least c + 1 days before.
hold[i] = max(hold[i-1], free[i-c-1] - prices[i]) and free[i] = max(free[i-1], hold[i-1] + prices[i]), treating free of a negative index as 0. The answer is free[n-1].
editorial: Use two arrays (or a rolling window). free[i] is the best profit at the end of day i without a share; hold[i] is the best profit at the end of day i while holding a share (the purchase price already subtracted). A sale on day i uses the holding state of day i-1 or earlier, so free[i] = max(free[i-1], hold[i-1] + prices[i]).

A purchase on day i is only legal if the last sale happened on day i - c - 1 or earlier. The best profit achievable under that condition is exactly free[i-c-1] (which already includes the option of having sold on that very day), so hold[i] = max(hold[i-1], free[i-c-1] - prices[i]). For i - c - 1 < 0 nothing has been sold yet, so the base is 0.

Each day costs O(1) work, giving O(n) time. Storing the whole free array uses O(n) memory; keeping only the last c + 1 values would reduce it to O(c). For c = 1 this is the classic three-state 'hold / just sold / rested' machine.
